title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that grounds a language model's answers in an external knowledge source. Instead of relying only on parameters learned during training, a RAG system retrieves relevant passages from a document collection at query time and passes them to the model as context. This reduces hallucination, keeps answers current without retraining, and lets the model cite its sources. A typical RAG pipeline has four stages: chunking documents, embedding the chunks, retrieving the most similar chunks for a query, and generating a grounded answer.

title: Vector Databases
text: A vector database stores high-dimensional embedding vectors and supports fast similarity search over them. Each item is represented as a dense vector, and queries are answered by finding the nearest vectors under a distance metric such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. Exact search compares the query against every stored vector, which is simple and accurate but scales linearly. Approximate nearest neighbour indexes such as HNSW or IVF trade a small amount of recall for large speed-ups, making search practical over millions of vectors. Popular vector databases include FAISS, Qdrant, Milvus, and pgvector.

title: Embeddings
text: An embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers that captures the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meanings map to nearby vectors, so semantic similarity becomes geometric proximity. Embeddings are produced by neural encoders trained on large corpora. In retrieval, both documents and queries are embedded into the same space so that a query can be matched to relevant documents by vector similarity. Embeddings are usually L2-normalised so that cosine similarity reduces to a dot product.

title: Chunking
text: Chunking splits long documents into smaller passages before embedding. Chunk size is a trade-off: passages that are too large dilute the relevant signal and waste context tokens, while passages that are too small lose the surrounding context needed to answer a question. A common strategy is to split on sentence boundaries and accumulate sentences up to a target size, carrying a small overlap between adjacent chunks so that facts spanning a boundary are not lost. Good chunking directly improves retrieval quality.

title: Model Routing and Token Optimisation
text: Model routing sends each request to the cheapest model capable of handling it, instead of using one large model for everything. Query complexity is estimated from signals such as length, reasoning cue words, question structure, and specificity. Simple factual lookups are routed to a small, inexpensive model, moderate questions to a mid-tier model, and complex multi-step reasoning to a premium model. Because most production traffic is easy, routing can cut total token cost substantially while preserving quality on the hard queries that need it. The savings are measured by comparing the cost actually spent against a baseline that always uses the premium model.

title: Claude Model Tiers
text: The Claude model family spans several capability and cost tiers. Haiku is the fastest and most cost-effective model, suited to simple, high-volume tasks. Sonnet offers a strong balance of speed and intelligence for most production workloads. Opus is the most capable tier for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Choosing the right tier per task is a core cost-optimisation lever: input and output tokens are priced per million, and premium tiers cost several times more than the cheapest tier.

title: Evaluating RAG Systems
text: Evaluating a RAG system means measuring both retrieval and generation. Retrieval metrics judge whether the right documents were fetched: hit-rate checks whether any relevant document appears in the results, recall@k measures the fraction of relevant documents retrieved, and mean reciprocal rank rewards placing a relevant document near the top. Generation metrics judge the final answer: exact match and token-level F1 compare the answer to a reference, and keyword coverage checks that required facts appear. A good harness reports both families together so retrieval and generation regressions can be told apart.

title: Cosine Similarity
text: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude. It ranges from -1 for opposite vectors to 1 for identical directions. For normalised vectors, cosine similarity equals the dot product, which makes it cheap to compute at scale. It is the default similarity metric in most retrieval systems because it compares direction rather than length, which suits embeddings where meaning is encoded in orientation.
